questions.title: How does the “absmean” quantization function determine the scaling factor γ?
questions.question_body: In the BitNet b1.58 paper the weight quantization is defined as \(\widetilde{W}=\mathrm{RoundClip}(W/(\gamma+\epsilon),-1,1)\) with \(\gamma = \frac{1}{nm}\sum_{ij}|W_{ij}|\). I am confused about why the authors use the average absolute value of the weight matrix as the scaling factor instead of, say, the maximum absolute value or RMS. How does this choice affect the distribution of ternary weights and the stability of training?

questions.title: Why are activations quantized to the symmetric range \([-Q_b, Q_b]\) instead of using a zero‑point offset?
questions.question_body: The paper states that activation quantization is performed per token to \([-Q_b, Q_b]\) to “get rid of the zero‑point quantization”. I don’t understand how removing the zero‑point simplifies implementation and whether it introduces any bias in the activation distribution. Could someone explain the trade‑offs between symmetric and asymmetric quantization in this context?

questions.title: What is the theoretical justification for calling a ternary weight model “1.58‑bit”?
questions.question_body: BitNet b1.58 uses weights taking values in \{-1,0,1\}. The authors claim this corresponds to 1.58 bits per weight in the binary system. How is this number derived (e.g., using entropy of a ternary distribution) and does it assume a particular probability of zero weights? Is there an alternative way to measure effective bit‑width for sparse ternary models?

questions.title: How does BitLinear replace nn.Linear while avoiding multiplications?
questions.question_body: The architecture replaces every \texttt{nn.Linear} with a custom \texttt{BitLinear}. I would like to see a concrete description of how matrix multiplication is carried out with ternary weights and 8‑bit activations using only integer additions. Does it involve separate add‑only kernels for positive and negative weights, or some form of popcount operation?

questions.title: Why does adding a zero value to the weight set improve ‘feature filtering’?
questions.question_body: The authors claim that adding the zero weight improves modeling capability because it enables explicit feature filtering. I am not clear on how a zero weight can act as a filter in transformer attention or feed‑forward layers. Can someone provide an intuitive explanation or a simple example illustrating this effect?

questions.title: What exactly is meant by the “new scaling law” introduced for 1.58‑bit LLMs?
questions.question_body: In Section 4 the paper mentions that BitNet b1.58 enables a new scaling law relating model performance and inference cost, and then lists heuristic equivalences (e.g., 13B BitNet ≈ 3B FP16). Is there a formal mathematical expression for this scaling law, or is it purely empirical? How should one extrapolate it to unseen model sizes or token counts?

questions.title: How were latency and memory measurements performed with the 2‑bit kernel from Ladder?
questions.question_body: "Both latency and memory were measured with a 2‑bit kernel, so there is still room for optimization…" I’m trying to understand what exactly was measured: was it the time for a single matrix‑multiply using Ladder’s kernel, or end‑to‑end inference time per token? Also, does using a 2‑bit kernel artificially inflate latency compared to an ideal 1‑bit implementation?

questions.title: What energy model was used to claim a 71.4× reduction in arithmetic operation energy?
questions.question_body: The paper cites energy models from \cite{energycost, pokebnn} and reports a 71.4× saving for matrix multiplication on 7nm chips. I would like clarification on which technology parameters (e.g., energy per FP16 add/mul vs INT8 add) were used, and whether memory access energy was included in this estimate.

questions.title: Can BitNet b1.58 be combined with Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) without changing the MoE routing algorithm?
questions.,question_body: The discussion suggests that 1.58‑bit models could alleviate MoE’s memory overhead, but it’s unclear whether the gating network and expert selection need to be quantized differently. Does applying ternary weights to experts affect routing stability or capacity allocation?

questions.title: What challenges remain for deploying BitNet b1.58 on edge CPUs?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that 1.58‑bit LLMs are more CPU‑friendly, yet modern mobile CPUs lack efficient int8 add only units for large matrix multiplies. What hardware primitives are required (e.g., SIMD instructions, bit‑serial arithmetic) and what software stack support (e.g., ONNX Runtime extensions) would enable practical inference on phones?
